parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator every thermal incident involving overheating, thermal runaway, fire, or explosion, including events without injury or property damage, within 5 business days of learning of it. A death, serious injury, or event presenting an imminent risk to the public must be reported within 24 hours.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator every thermal incident involving overheating, thermal runaway, fire, or explosion, including events without injury or property damage, within 5 business days of learning of it. A death, serious injury, or event presenting an imminent risk to the public must be reported within 24 hours.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator every thermal incident involving overheating, thermal runaway, fire, or explosion, including events without injury or property damage, within 5 business days of learning of it. A death, serious injury, or event presenting an imminent risk to the public must be reported within 24 hours. Within 30 days, the manufacturer must provide a follow-up with known causes and corrective actions. Affected customers must be notified within 5 business days of identifying a material risk to their unit, and immediately when urgent action is needed. Reports must include model, event date, location, known circumstances, and any injury or damage; regulators may request further information.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A result above a 5% failure rate requires a corrective-action plan and regulator review, but does not automatically prohibit sale; regulators may require further testing or impose restrictions where results indicate an unreasonable safety risk.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Before sale, after material design changes, and annually thereafter, manufacturers must submit per-model results, test methods, sample sizes, and corrective actions to the relevant regulator, and make the results available to customers who buy that model. Results need not be disclosed to the general public. A result above a 5% failure rate requires a corrective-action plan and regulator review, but does not automatically prohibit sale; regulators may require further testing or impose restrictions where results indicate an unreasonable safety risk. Regulators should review the threshold as evidence and testing methods develop.

parameters.quote: New units placed on the market from 3 years after this standard takes effect must support a secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. For installed units, manufacturers must provide a feasible retrofit or equivalent mitigation plan within 2 years, and complete required retrofits within 6 years of the standard taking effect.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New units placed on the market from 3 years after this standard takes effect must support a secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. For installed units, manufacturers must provide a feasible retrofit or equivalent mitigation plan within 2 years, and complete required retrofits within 6 years of the standard taking effect.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New units placed on the market from 3 years after this standard takes effect must support a secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation and clear customer instructions. For installed units, manufacturers must provide a feasible retrofit or equivalent mitigation plan within 2 years, and complete required retrofits within 6 years of the standard taking effect. Where a retrofit is not technically feasible, the manufacturer must notify affected customers and provide an alternative safety measure.

parameters.quote: New units placed on the market beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression designed and validated for the unit’s intended installation and use. Regulators may approve equivalent protective designs where they provide comparable risk reduction.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units placed on the market beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression designed and validated for the unit’s intended installation and use. Regulators may approve equivalent protective designs where they provide comparable risk reduction.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units placed on the market beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression designed and validated for the unit’s intended installation and use. Manufacturers must provide installation, maintenance, and limitations information to customers. Regulators may approve equivalent protective designs where they provide comparable risk reduction.

parameters.quote: Per-model test results, including failure rates, must be made available to customers who buy that model and submitted to regulators; they need not be disclosed to the general public. When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using a consistent installed-unit denominator and regulator-verified data, regulators must promptly review the evidence and may require a recall or other corrective action based on incident severity, test results, and available mitigations.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: Per-model test results, including failure rates, must be made available to customers who buy that model and submitted to regulators; they need not be disclosed to the general public. When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using a consistent installed-unit denominator and regulator-verified data, regulators must promptly review the evidence and may require a recall or other corrective action based on incident severity, test results, and available mitigations.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must provide customers, at purchase and in accessible online materials, model-specific safety information, incident and emergency-response instructions, required maintenance, relevant test methods, and a summary of applicable safety testing. Per-model test results, including failure rates, must be made available to customers who buy that model and submitted to regulators; they need not be disclosed to the general public. When a manufacturer identifies a material safety risk, it must promptly notify affected customers with the nature of the risk, actions to take, and support contacts; urgent risks require immediate notice. Manufacturers must notify regulators of corrective-action plans. When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, using a consistent installed-unit denominator and regulator-verified data, regulators must promptly review the evidence and may require a recall or other corrective action based on incident severity, test results, and available mitigations. Regulators may order a recall sooner when they determine that a model presents an unreasonable safety risk.

judge_section_notes: The final rules are a mixed package: S1 is strong on reporting timelines and scope; S2 keeps the 55°C test and a 5% corrective-action threshold but no automatic sales stop, with per-model results to buyers but not the public; S3 delays new-unit shut-off to 3 years and retrofit to 6 years; S4 requires built-in suppression at 36 months with equivalent designs allowed; S5 makes the 8/100k level a trigger for regulator review rather than mandatory recall. Both red lines are formally respected, but Northwind gains more from S2/S3 while Halcyon gains from S5.
